title: 25 Things to Do After Work Instead of Scrolling, With a Kit for Each Kind of Evening
dek: Twenty-five weeknight ideas sorted by how you feel, each one easy to start because the small thing it needs is already on the shelf.

body.text: Scrolling after work isn't a character flaw. It's the easiest thing within reach when your brain is tired, and that's the whole problem: the alternative has to be almost as easy.

Here are twenty-five ideas that fit inside a normal weeknight, sorted by how you feel when you clock out: creative, exhausted, in need of people, or with a little energy left. Most come with one small kit that makes them easy to start. Pick one, not all of them.
If you want to make something

body.title: Paint whatever is on your counter
body.note: Grab a small watercolor set and paint your mug, a lemon or the flowers on the table. Twenty minutes, three colors, no erasing. The [watercolor](/journal/watercolor-painting-for-beginners) guide shows you where to begin. **What makes it easier:** a travel watercolor set and a pad of heavier paper, so twenty minutes becomes a finished little page.

body.title: Make a clay ring dish
body.note: Air-dry clay doesn't need a kiln. Roll a ball, press your thumb in, smooth the edges and let it dry (about a day to the touch for Crayola's, longer for thick pieces; check your clay's label), then paint it. [Here's how to start](/journal/how-to-start-air-dry-clay). **What makes it easier:** a tub of air-dry clay, a small set of sculpting tools and a craft mat, so the table stays clean and the edges come out crisp.

body.title: Start a junk journal page
body.note: Empty your bag. Receipts, tickets, the coffee sleeve. Glue three of them into a notebook with a line about your week. **What makes it easier:** {{product:stationery-island-a5-blank-journal-180-pages|a thick-paged notebook}}, a glue stick and a few rolls of {{product:mr-pen-washi-tape-21-rolls|washi tape}}, so the receipts and tickets become a page in minutes.

body.title: Bake something to give away
body.note: Cookies are a forty-minute project, and giving half to a neighbor or coworker is half the fun.

body.title: Write a letter to a friend
body.note: An actual letter, on paper, with a stamp. It takes fifteen minutes and makes someone's whole week. **What makes it easier:** a small letter-writing set with paper, cards and envelopes, so the letter is ready to post.

steps: Put your phone on the charger in another room.
Clear one corner of the kitchen table.
Set a 30-minute timer and make something with what you have: a small watercolor set, a block of clay, or a notebook and some glue.
When the timer goes off, you're allowed to stop. You probably won't want to.

body.title: For a make-something evening
body.dek: A travel watercolor set, a block of clay, a thick-paged journal and a letter-writing set, kept in one drawer so starting takes seconds.

body.text: If most evenings feel like this, our guide to [low-energy hobbies](/journal/low-energy-hobbies) has more gentle ideas.

body.title: Do a puzzle with a podcast
body.note: Put on a podcast or an album and work on a jigsaw for half an hour. Your hands stay busy, your eyes get a break, and you can stop whenever you like. **What makes it easier:** a jigsaw puzzle on a tray or mat, so the pieces move off the table in one go when you need it back.

body.title: Read in a different room
body.note: Take your book somewhere that isn't your bed or your desk. A bath, a balcony, the floor in a patch of light. It makes reading feel like a little event. **What makes it easier:** a clip-on book light, so you can read in a dim corner without lighting the whole room.

body.title: Paint by numbers
body.note: No blank canvas, no decisions. Do just one color tonight and leave the rest for another evening. **What makes it easier:** a paint-by-number kit that includes the paints and a brush, so there is nothing to gather before the first color.

body.title: Make a 'nice' dinner for one
body.note: Light a candle, use the good plate, eat at the table. The meal can be pasta. The point is treating your own Tuesday like it matters. **Nice to have:** a set of flameless LED candles and a small tea set, so the table looks like an occasion without any fuss.

body.title: For a nothing-left evening
body.dek: A puzzle, a paint-by-number kit, a clip-on light and a soft throw: the small things that make the sofa the easy option.

body.title: Host a 90-minute craft hour
body.note: Not a dinner party. Just a table, snacks and a bracelet kit, a first [crochet](/journal/how-to-start-crocheting) square or an [embroidery](/journal/how-to-start-embroidery) hoop. Text two friends 'craft hour Thursday?', which is easier to say yes to than a big plan. [How to host a craft night](/journal/how-to-host-a-craft-night) has the plan. **What makes it easier:** a friendship bracelet kit or a beginner kit for each person, so nobody arrives to an empty table.

body.title: Start a standing game night
body.note: Mahjong, cards, a cooperative board game. Same night every week or every other week, so nobody has to plan. If it is mahjong, see [how to host a mahjong night](/journal/how-to-host-a-mahjong-night). **What makes it easier:** a board game or an American mahjong set, so the same box comes out on the same night each week.

body.text: If you still have some energy

body.title: Play pickleball or tennis
body.note: Many public courts have lights for evening play; check your parks department for hours and any booking fees. New to either? Start with [pickleball for beginners](/journal/pickleball-for-beginners) or [tennis as an adult](/journal/how-to-start-playing-tennis-as-an-adult). **What makes it easier:** a starter paddle set or a beginner racket and a water bottle, so a spontaneous evening game just needs a friend.

body.title: Do a sunset photo walk
body.note: Give yourself a theme, like 'red things' or 'windows,' and photograph twenty examples before the light goes. **Worth bringing:** comfortable walking shoes and a phone armband, so your hands stay free for the twenty photos.

body.title: For evenings with friends or a little energy
body.dek: A painting kit, a board game, a bracelet kit, a paddle set and a bottle: one box for the group and one bag for the court.

body.text: Willpower is the wrong tool. Change the friction instead. Leave the hobby out where you'll see it, since a puzzle on the table gets used and a kit in a closet doesn't. Charge your phone in the kitchen for the first hour after you get home. Decide your evening at lunchtime, when you're not tired. And lower the bar: twenty minutes counts, and so does one page. Many of these are [affordable hobbies](/journal/affordable-hobbies-under-25).
Choosing is the hard part on a tired Tuesday. Make Some Plans can turn your energy and the hours you really have into one small plan you can save.
Seven ways in that need nothing but the evening, and then a few places to go.

body.title: Take a slow evening walk
body.note: No step count, no destination. Walk until something catches your eye, then walk home. Bring a phone for safety, not for scrolling. **Worth bringing:** walking shoes you like and a phone armband for music, so you can set off without thinking.

body.title: Rearrange one shelf
body.note: Style one shelf with books, a plant and something you've thrifted. A small home project can scratch the creative itch without a big commitment.

body.title: Run one weeknight errand the scenic way
body.note: Walk to the farther grocery store, the one by the park. A small detour can turn a chore into a little outing. **Worth bringing:** a market tote for the groceries, so the long way home is easy to carry.

body.title: Cook with a friend
body.note: One of you brings a recipe, the other brings the ingredients. You eat what you make and wash up together.

body.title: Call someone instead of texting
body.note: Go for a walk and call a friend you've been 'meaning to catch up with' for months.

body.title: Learn something tiny
body.note: A new knot, a calligraphy alphabet, three phrases in a language for your next trip. Small skills feel big. **Worth bringing:** a set of brush pens or a pocket notebook, so the new alphabet or knot gets written down.

body.title: Plan your weekend on paper
body.note: Grab a planner and sketch out one fun thing for Saturday and one for Sunday. Having something to look forward to changes how the rest of the week feels. **Worth bringing:** a pocket notebook or planner, so Saturday's one fun thing is somewhere you will see it.

body.text: Borrow a library book or a neighbor's puzzle first if you like. Your own copy, a clip-on light and a good pair of walking shoes make the second evening easier.

body.title: Take a drop-in class
body.note: Pottery, life drawing, dance, yoga. Many studios offer single drop-in sessions, so check their schedules and try without committing.

body.title: Go to an adult skate night
body.note: Some rinks run adults-only evenings, so check your local rink's schedule. You will wobble. Everybody wobbles. **What makes it easier:** skate protective gear of your own, so you can step onto the rink ready.

body.title: Join a library book club
body.note: Libraries often host free book clubs (check your local branch), and some bookstores do too. Showing up once is a fine start.

body.title: Go to a museum's late night
body.note: Some museums stay open late one evening a week, sometimes with free or lower-priced entry. Check your local museum's calendar. **Worth bringing:** a pocket notebook for the details you want to keep.

body.title: Have a solo dinner out
body.note: Sit at the bar or by the window with a book. A table for one is an easy plan to say yes to.
